Limb-onset ALS is top consideration given its typical presentation: insidious onset, progressive weakness/atrophy in distal upper limbs, often with fasciculations and eventual upper motor neuron signs; early bulbar/respiratory sparing is common. SMA type III fits well—childhood-to-adult onset, proximal > distal weakness, slow progression, no sensory involvement, and preserved bulbar/respiratory function until late stages. MMN is strongly considered due to its hallmark of purely motor, asymmetric, slowly progressive limb weakness with conduction block on NCS—often misdiagnosed as ALS but treatable with IVIG. Late-onset SMA (type IV) overlaps clinically with type III but presents after age 30 and may be underrecognized. CMT1A is included but lower confidence because it typically includes sensory symptoms and foot deformities; pure motor presentations occur but are atypical—hence lower weight. Excluded: myasthenia gravis (bulbar/respiratory involvement common, fatigability), inflammatory myopathies (proximal > distal, CK elevation, no atrophy early), and cervical spondylotic myelopathy (usually spasticity, sensory level, reflex changes—not isolated atrophic weakness)."}
